headline: Sequoia's Global Dreams Die Quietly, Locally
subheadline: The firm that spent two decades expanding worldwide announces it was wrong and is going home, while somehow raising $10 billion to do it.
source_headline: Sequoia hits rewind, undoing 20 years of expansion
body_html:
Sequoia Capital, the venture firm that spent the better part of two decades convincing limited partners that being everywhere was the future, is now announcing that being everywhere was, in fact, a mistake. The consolidation will shutter programs and offices built during its ambitious global expansion, while the firm somehow managed to raise approximately $10 billion in new capital to fund this strategic retreat. Nothing says "we learned our lesson" like raising your largest fund yet to fix the problems created by raising large funds everywhere.

For two decades, Sequoia sold a compelling narrative: venture capital knows no borders, and neither should Sequoia. The firm planted flags across continents, opened regional offices, hired local partners, and generally performed the theatrical expansion that convinced everyone—from LPs to founders to business journalists—that geographic footprint equaled competitive advantage. The logic was intoxicating: why miss opportunities in London, Shanghai, or Mumbai when you could be present in all three simultaneously? It turns out that being present and being effective are not the same thing, a distinction that apparently required 20 years and significant capital depletion to clarify.

This is not Sequoia's first encounter with the "global strategy" mirage. The venture industry has cycled through this exact pattern before: expansion becomes fashionable, firms race outward, synergies fail to materialize, and then—quietly, without dramatic press releases—the programs get closed and capital gets redeployed. The difference now is scale and timing: Sequoia's consolidation is happening during a moment when other mega-firms are still telling their LPs that mega-funds and mega-footprints are the only viable strategy for mega-returns. Sequoia is undoing 20 years of hype while raising $10 billion that explicitly contradicts those two decades of messaging.

The firm's statement likely emphasizes "focus" and "operational excellence," which in VC vernacular means "we got distracted and it didn't work." Expect language about returning to core competencies, doubling down on expertise, and building deeper rather than wider—all of which translate to: we should have stayed home. The Bay Area–centered model they're returning to is precisely what made Sequoia relevant before the global expansion began. They're not pivoting; they're admitting they were wrong and hoping no one notices they're charging the same management fees for it.

The question haunting LPs in Sequoia's new $10 billion fund is straightforward: if the firm spent 20 years building a global machine and then concluded the entire experiment was misguided, what confidence can we have that this new capital will be deployed correctly? The track record suggests that even elite investors make generational-scale bets based on herd mentality and fashion. Sequoia expanded globally because everyone was doing it. Now everyone is consolidating, so Sequoia is consolidating. The pattern itself should concern any thoughtful allocator.

Sequoia's rewind is a bellwether moment for venture capital's maturity—or lack thereof. An industry that prides itself on backing founders who "learn from failure" is run by fund managers who rarely experience consequences for their own strategic errors. When the strategy fails, capital is simply reallocated and the narrative is rewritten. Sequoia isn't shrinking; it's rebranding its contraction as enlightenment. Meanwhile, LPs are writing checks for the privilege of learning yesterday's lessons at tomorrow's fees.

The real synergy here isn't in geographic footprint—it's in the synchronous ability of venture capital to be confidently wrong, then confidently right about the opposite, and somehow raise more capital for both.
glossary_definition: A 20-year bet that spray-painting your brand across three continents somehow creates competitive advantage; empirically disproven but fundable for one cycle.
